extracted.intended_audience: War Department officials, military pay administrators, auditors, and military/labor attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Collection of legal standards and administrative rulings governing entitlement to pay, allowances, commutation, and related benefits for U.S. Army officers and enlisted men (extra-duty pay, quarters, heat/light, forage, clothing, transportation, interment, etc.). Intended to guide pay/accounting decisions and legal interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extra-duty pay — department relation
rubrics_metrics.description: An enlisted man is not entitled to extra-duty pay for the performance of duty pertaining to the department to which he belongs; if, however, he renders service in another staff department, having no relation to the duties required of him in his own department, he may properly receive extra-duty pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 25352, July 31, 1909. (Distinguishes ordinary duty within one's department from unrelated service in another staff department as basis for extra-duty compensation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Cook extra compensation — applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: Army regulation providing for payment from the company fund of the extra compensation of 25 cents per day to enlisted men who are cooks has reference to ordinary enlisted men and does not apply to persons enlisted under the act of July 7, 1898, as cooks with the rank and pay of corporals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 4762, Aug., 1898. (Rule limits the regulation to ordinary enlisted cooks, excluding statutory special enlistments with rank/pay equivalence.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of extra-duty pay — self-sustaining activities
rubrics_metrics.description: When enlisted men were paid for extra duty as messengers in operation of a post laundry from the receipts for laundry work, such extra-duty pay was properly paid from such receipts where the law required the entire cost of operation to be paid from receipts before surplus deposited to appropriation credit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 28968, Sept. 13, 1911. (Payments from enterprise receipts are permissible where statute/regulation dedicates receipts to operation costs.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of wartime statute on extra-duty pay
rubrics_metrics.description: War between the United States and Spain as declared by act of Congress approved April 22, 1898, existed when the act of April 26, 1898, was passed. Held that enlisted men in all departments ceased to be entitled to extra-duty pay upon the date of the approval of the last-named act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 4089, 4135, 4143, 4144, May, 1898; 4256, June, 1898. (Statutory changes in wartime may terminate prior extra-duty entitlements as of the act's approval date.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 6 (Apr 26,1898) — source limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 6 of the act of April 26, 1898 ... in providing that in war time no additional increased compensation (i.e., additional to the twenty per centum increase) shall be allowed to soldiers performing what is known as extra or special duty, applies to increased compensation made directly from appropriations for the support of the Army and not to payments made from the company, bakery, or post exchange funds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 4414, 4539, 4540, 5442, June to Dec, 1898; 5661, Jan., 1899; 20121, July 25, 1906; 20152, July 31, 1906. (Distinguishes appropriations-funded compensation from fund-source payments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of other appropriations to pay extra duty
rubrics_metrics.description: Where appropriations are made for work other than that covered by the items for extra-duty pay, enlisted men may, under proper restrictions, be employed on extra duty thereon and paid extra compensation from such appropriation, even though the appropriation itself does not specify payments for extra-duty services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 15827, Feb. 2, 1904; O. 19038, Jan. 11, 1906. (Authority may select means of accomplishing authorized work and compensate enlisted men instead of contracting civilian labor.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit for purchase of discharge — forfeiture on desertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a soldier deposited $50 under the act of May 15, 1872, presumably in anticipation of his application for purchase of discharge, and subsequently while such application was pending deserted, said deposit was necessarily unconditional and like any other deposit was forfeited by desertion.

rubrics_metrics.name: No authority to refund purchase-of-discharge money
rubrics_metrics.description: There was no legal authority for the refunding, by the military authorities, of money paid to purchase a discharge under the act of June 16, 1890; the act provides that the money when paid 'shall be deposited in the Treasury' to the credit of the appropriation for pay of the Army and authorizes the President to permit such purchases 'under such rules and upon such conditions as he shall prescribe' — nothing found to allow refunding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allotments voluntary
rubrics_metrics.description: Both allotments and discontinuances of allotments by soldiers are voluntary and entirely within the discretion of the soldier making them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 11403, Nov. 9, 1901. (Administrative rule emphasizing soldier's autonomy over allotments.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat and light as allowance in kind — scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of March 2, 1907, creates an allowance in kind, as distinguished from one which can be commuted in money ... Held that heat and light cannot be furnished at any other place or to any other building than that occupied by the officer or enlisted man at his post of duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, Mar. 6, 1907; Jan. 21, 1909; Dec. 16, 1911. (Heat/light are tied to actual quarters occupied at station.)

rubrics_metrics.name: War Dept duty to furnish heat and light; method discretionary
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of March 2, 1907, is positive in its requirements, and charges the War Department with the duty of providing heat and light for the quarters lawfully occupied by commissioned officers and enlisted men. The statute is silent as to the method and places no limitation on cost; details are committed to the discretion of the Secretary of War.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, Aug. 27, 1908. (Operational details left to Quartermaster/Secretary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to quarters accrual
rubrics_metrics.description: The right to quarters accrues in behalf of an officer in the operation of an order from competent authority assigning him to a particular post or place for duty. The duty of heating and lighting is charged to the Quartermaster's Department only where an officer at the station to which he has been regularly assigned has been provided with quarters in kind, or, there being no such quarters available, has been allowed commutation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 22467, Dec. 9, 1907. (Assignment/official station triggers quarters rights.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat/light are in-kind allowances paid to suppliers
rubrics_metrics.description: The furnishing of heat and light is in the nature of an allowance in kind, and is not an allowance payable to an officer in money ... payments when due are not made to the officer who occupies quarters or obtains them in the operation of commutation, but to persons who furnish heat, light, fuel, or illuminants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, May 9 and June 4, 1910. (Payments go to providers, not the occupant.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary change for treatment does not alter entitlement
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer in receipt of commutation of quarters who was ordered to Hot Springs, Ark., for treatment was held not to change status; he continued to be entitled to heat and light at his permanent station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, Apr. 18, 1907. (Temporary medical orders do not alter quarters/heat-light status at permanent station.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank-limited furnishing (Philippine Constabulary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Heat and light could lawfully be furnished for such rooms only as the Chief and Assistant Chiefs of Philippine Constabulary are entitled to by virtue of their actual rank; any additional allowance must come from the Philippine Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, June 26, 1907. (Limits allowances to entitlement by U.S. rank; local government pays extras.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion and accrual of rights to rooms and heat/light
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer promoted is entitled to pay and commutation of quarters from the date of promotion (date of vacancy); he is entitled to occupy rooms appropriate to new grade from same date and Quartermaster would be charged with furnishing heat and light for additional room from the date of the vacancy, provided room actually used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, May 9; June 4, 1910; Apr. 1, 1911. (Rights accrue with promotion/vacancy date.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Entitlement while on leave retaining quarters
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an officer received a leave of absence retaining his quarters during the period of such leave, the quarters were standing in his name and he was, theoretically at least, occupying them; the officer is entitled to his allowance of heat and light while on leave of absence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, Sept. 4, 1909; Feb. 4, 1911. (Holding that holding/retaining quarters preserves allowance rights.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Quartermaster duty when lease/custom excludes heat/light
rubrics_metrics.description: If the local practice in renting is to include heat and light, or if the lease or the rates paid call for it, the requirements of the statute are satisfied; otherwise heat and light should be stipulated for in the lease in order that proper execution may be given to the statute (act of Mar. 2, 1907).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, Aug. 27, 1908. (Administrative guidance to ensure leases provide heat/light when needed.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commute-of-rations does not defeat heat/light right
rubrics_metrics.description: The Quartermaster General is charged by law with furnishing heat and light to quarters furnished to officers and enlisted men, and it is the opinion of this office that the right of the enlisted men is not defeated and the duty of the Quartermaster's Department is not diminished by the fact that commutation of rations is paid to the soldier by the Subsistence Department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, Jan. 11, 1909. (Coordination among departments; suggests amending regulations if unclear.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlisted men outside reservation not entitled to heat/light as of right
rubrics_metrics.description: An enlisted man living outside the military reservation on which he is serving as a soldier is not entitled, as of right, to heat and light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 19126, Dec. 28, 1909. (Physical location relative to reservation limits entitlement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction on sale of fuel/light materials
rubrics_metrics.description: In view of the provisions of successive appropriation acts impliedly restricting the selling by the United States of material for fuel and light to sales to 'officers,' and of the previous practice to that effect, such sales should not be permitted to be made to other classes of persons until Congress shall have so authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 58, 470, Apr., 1893. (Statutory/appropriation constraint on whom government may sell fuel.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of station — transportation of horses
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer ordered from Fort Custer to Washington, D. C., to await retirement, but not in fact retired till about five months after arrival, was entitled to the regulation allowance for the transportation of his horses from Fort Custer, on the ground that he was changing station; Washington became his proper station and he was entitled to allowances accruing to an officer at his station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 60, 22, June, 1893. (Interim station status confers station-based allowances.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Transporting purchased horses — cost limitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Quartermaster's Department will transport horses purchased at points other than their station, provided the cost of shipment from point of purchase to new station does not exceed the cost of shipment from the old to new station on last change of station, and provided the officer has not had his authorized private mounts shipped from his old to his new station; if cost would exceed, shipping at government expense is not legal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 24000, Aug. 5, 1911. (Objective cost comparison and prior shipment history condition.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Indian agent detail — commutation inapplicable
rubrics_metrics.description: An officer of the Army, acting as Indian agent, occupying as his quarters, without rent, a house at the agency placed at his disposal by the Interior Department, was not entitled to commutation of quarters; detail as Indian agent detaches him from military duty and places him under the Secretary of the Interior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 64, 121, Mar., 1894; G. 12939, July 25, 1902; 14574, Jan. 8, 1910. (Detachment to non-military office affects entitlement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Secretary of War discretion to assign station and commutation
rubrics_metrics.description: It is within the power of the Secretary of War to assign an officer to any military duty and to give him a station at any place ... to meet the case of an officer mapping the country, it is only necessary to assign the officer to duty at a place convenient to his work; as there are no public quarters at such place, he becomes entitled to commutation. Authority to permit family to remain is within Secretary's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 17407, Jan. 18, 1905. (Operational flexibility subject to Secretary's discretion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequent travel stops — entitlement during stops
rubrics_metrics.description: If an officer not in the field is on a duty that requires him to travel, and finds it necessary to make frequent stops varying in length from a few days to a few weeks, he is entitled during such stops to either quarters in kind or commutation of quarters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 18963, Sept. 30, 1904. (Short-duration travel stops qualify for temporary quarters/commutation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Interment allowance — not payable when officer on sick leave
rubrics_metrics.description: The regulation allowance for the expenses of the interment of an officer was not payable in a case of an officer who at the time of his death was on sick leave, this not being one of the cases specified in the Army appropriation acts in which such allowance is authorized to be paid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 60, 47, June, 1893; C. 6126, Mar. 27, 1899; 13598, Nov. 11, 1902. (Statutory specificity controls payment.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Permanent interment authorization — conditions and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The fact that an officer had been interred at the post where he died does not preclude the Secretary of War from authorizing his permanent interment elsewhere, provided the entire expenses of burial do not exceed the maximum amount allowed (e.g., $75) and the officer was on duty at time of death; not allowed if he died while on sick leave away from station.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 65, 183, June, 1894; C. 13598, Nov. 11, 1902. (Expense cap and duty-status preconditions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forage allowances — ownership and actual keeping
rubrics_metrics.description: The acts of June 18, 1878 and Feb. 24, 1881 regulate the issue of forage to officers, who become entitled to the allowance only for horses owned and actually kept 'in the performance of their official military duties.' A subaltern officer who owns one horse may draw forage for one; if he owns two and the conditions are met, he may draw for two.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 24000, Oct. 23, 1908. (Strict ownership/use test governs forage entitlement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mar 2, 1907 and forage acts — no impairment
rubrics_metrics.description: The act of March 2, 1907 was never intended to impair the efficiency of the acts of 1878 and 1881 regulating forage allowances for mounted officers; public animals issued to officers continue to be foraged and cared for by the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 23277, Feb. 16, 1909. (Preserves prior forage regime against later statute misinterpretation.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Retired officer detailed as professor — no forage
rubrics_metrics.description: A retired officer detailed as professor at an educational institution is not entitled to a forage allowance, as the duty upon which he is placed is not one which requires him to be mounted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 23957, Oct. 28, 1911. (Character of duty, not rank, determines forage entitlement.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Contractor/arranged-forage schemes invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: A contract surgeon who arranged for horses to be nominally owned by officers (e.g., bills of sale for $1) and had forage drawn against officers' allowances did not create lawful entitlement; the law allows forage only to mounted officers for horses 'owned and actually kept' by such officers 'in the performance of their official military duties.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 23277, Feb. 16, 1909. (Substance over form; sham transfers not recognized.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between pay and allowances upon dismissal
rubrics_metrics.description: A dismissal of an officer by order of the President does not involve a deprivation of any part of the pay due him; if the order is so expressed as to dismiss him 'without pay or allowances' it is, as to this portion, unauthorized and inoperative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 10, 216, Aug., 1864; R. 42, 470, Jan. 19, 1880. (Vested pay rights cannot be nullified by executive phrasing.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Pay/allowances and misconduct/absence
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay and allowances are given to a soldier because he earns them or is, without fault on his part and by circumstances not within his control, prevented from doing so; when pay is withheld because he (by his own fault) failed to earn it, his clothing allowance should be withheld for the same reason. Thus a soldier absent without leave or in the hands of civil authorities serving sentence should not be allowed either pay or clothing allowance for the period of such unauthorized absence from duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 12025, Feb. 6, 1902; 2010, Feb., 1896; 14642, May 22, 1903; 17518, Feb. 13, 1905; 16966, July 17, 1905. (Fault-based withholding applies equally to pay and related allowances.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeiture of clothing allowance during confinement
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier sentenced to confinement with forfeiture of all pay and allowances for six months who drew clothing while serving the sentence forfeited his clothing allowance during the period of confinement and it was proper to charge the drawn clothing against his clothing allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 1525, July, 1895. (Administrative practice of charging issues against forfeited allowances.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Clothing issued remains U.S. property; accounting charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Clothing issued to soldiers for use in the military service continues to be the property of the United States — the practice of charging them with the money value on issue is required by statute for convenience in accounting and to incite economy in use and care of clothing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: R. 45, 552, Jan. 20, 1883; P. 51, 159, Dec. 30, 1891; C. 11251, May 12, 1910; 16107, Sept. 20, 1911; 21179, Dec. 23, 1911. (Treats clothing as public property for legal/accounting purposes.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge without honor — excess clothing not allowed
rubrics_metrics.description: When a soldier is discharged without honor because of fraudulent enlistment, he should not be permitted to take clothing with him which has been drawn in excess of his allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 2113, Mar. 9, 1896; 7782, Mar. 6, 1900; 11251, Sept. 24, 1901; 16048, Mar. 19, 1904. (Sanctions on improper retention upon dishonorable discharge.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Returning deserter cannot reclaim clothing left behind
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon the return of a deserter to military control he cannot claim as private property articles of uniform clothing which had been issued to him before his desertion and which he left behind at desertion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 3251, June 2, 1899; 21179, Mar. 7, 1907; 29407, Jan. 30, 1912. (Public-property status persists despite desertion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Gratuitous issues for destruction to prevent contagion only
rubrics_metrics.description: Circular 57, A. G. O., 1898 provides that whenever articles of clothing of enlisted men have been destroyed to prevent contagion a gratuitous issue of such articles will be made ... Held that there was no provision for paying for the clothing destroyed in lieu of the gratuitous issue authorized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 5588, Jan., 1899; 20143, Aug. 3 and 16, 1906. (Relief by issue, not cash payment; regulations may allow limited gratuitous issues for extreme climates/campaigns.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss by fire/casualty — reimbursement route
rubrics_metrics.description: A soldier is not entitled to be credited in his clothing account with the value of clothing lost by fire or other casualty; this can be made good to him only through the reimbursement authorized by the act of March 3, 1885.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 63, 278, Jan., 1894; C. 10025, Mar. 22, 1901; 20143, Aug. 2, 16, Sept. 21, 1906; Oct. 13, 1910. (Statutory reimbursement procedure is exclusive remedy.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen's outer clothing on release — confinement prerequisite
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision in an Army appropriation act 'for a suit of citizen's outer clothing ... to be issued upon release from confinement to each prisoner who has been confined under a court-martial sentence involving dishonorable discharge' did not apply where the sentence adjudged dishonorable discharge without any term of confinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: C. 2925, Feb. 9, 1897, and Jan. 5, 1912; 14256, Mar. 12, 1903. (Confinement required by statutory language.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Commutation of rations for travel — limited to travel period
rubrics_metrics.description: The allowance for commutation of rations made payable by the Army appropriation act to enlisted men traveling on detached duty 'when it is impracticable to carry rations' is restricted to the period covered by the travel, and not payable to a soldier for commutation of rations consumed at the destination where he was placed by his orders (e.g., hotel board at terminus).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: P. 59, 38, Apr., 1893. (Commutation is travel-limited, not destination-subsistence.)
